word:greek-nt:G0053.explanation: Hagnos means pure. It can also describe chastity, as in a pure virgin.

word:greek-nt:G0138.explanation: Haireō means to choose or prefer. It can describe choosing one course rather than another.

word:greek-nt:G0174.explanation: Akanthinos means made of thorns, or thorny.

word:greek-nt:G0246.explanation: This Greek New Testament word refers to a foreigner or Gentile—someone viewed as belonging to another people rather than one’s own. It identifies a person by their national or people-group identity, not by a personal name or individual quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 10:28, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G0291.explanation: Ampliatus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears one time, in Romans 16:8. The name itself does not provide a further meaning or description of the person; understanding his identity and significance requires the surrounding biblical context, which is not included here. Its use is therefore best understood simply as the proper name Ampliatus.

word:greek-nt:G0347.explanation: Anaklinō means to lay down or make someone recline.

word:greek-nt:G0440.explanation: Anthrax means coal or a burning coal.

word:greek-nt:G0505.explanation: Anypokritos means sincere or genuine, without hypocrisy.

word:greek-nt:G0549.explanation: Apeimi means to go away or depart.

word:greek-nt:G0624.explanation: Apollonia is the name of a place. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, in Acts 17:1, and refers to the town visited during the journey described there. As a proper name, it does not express an action, quality, or spiritual concept by itself; it identifies a specific location. The name is rendered consistently as “Apollonia.” Its exact significance in the surrounding account comes from the passage’s narrative, while the word itself simply names the place.

word:greek-nt:G0651.explanation: Apostolē means apostleship—the commission or duty of an apostle.

word:greek-nt:G0668.explanation: Apopheugō means to flee from or escape.

word:greek-nt:G0888.explanation: Achreios means unprofitable or useless. It can also describe a servant as unworthy.

word:greek-nt:G0992.explanation: Bletēos means must be put or ought to be put.

word:greek-nt:G1029.explanation: Brochos means a noose or snare, something that can ensnare or restrain.

word:greek-nt:G1065.explanation: Ge is an emphasizing particle, adding force to a statement with the sense “indeed,” “really,” or “at least.”

word:greek-nt:G1160.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “cost”—the amount that must be paid for something. It names the required expense or price rather than describing the act of paying itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 14:28. Its basic sense draws attention to what something will require before a person undertakes it; the specific force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual wording.

word:greek-nt:G1362.explanation: Diplous means double or twofold, that is, twice as much.

word:greek-nt:G1494.explanation: Hierothutos means meat sacrificed to an image or idol.

word:greek-nt:G1599.explanation: This word means “to send away,” “to send away/out,” or “to send out.” It describes the action of dispatching someone or sending them away from one place to another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains movement caused by someone sending another person onward or away.

word:greek-nt:G1807.explanation: Exaireō means to take out or remove. It can also mean to rescue or deliver, as when a person is delivered from affliction.

word:greek-nt:G1890.explanation: This word means “to foam up,” describing something that rises and froths like bubbling foam. It is a vivid verb for turbulent, agitated movement rather than a quiet or settled condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:13. Its ordinary sense centers on foaming or frothing outward, and the surrounding verse supplies the specific comparison or force intended there.

word:greek-nt:G1942.explanation: Epikalymma means a cloak or covering; it can describe a cloak of wickedness.

word:greek-nt:G2011.explanation: This word means “commission”: an authorized assignment or charge given to someone. It refers to being entrusted with a task to carry out, rather than merely receiving general advice or information. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on an assigned responsibility or authorization to act.

word:greek-nt:G2028.explanation: This word means “to name,” “to be called,” or “to call” someone by a name. It describes the act of giving a name or identifying a person through what he or she is called. In ordinary Bible language, it functions as a verb rather than as the name itself. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Romans 2:17, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the act of naming or being called.

word:greek-nt:G2064.explanation: Erchomai means to come, describing people who come to worship and a shower that is said to be coming.

word:greek-nt:G2200.explanation: Hot describes something having a high temperature. It is an adjective, used to identify a condition or quality rather than an action or person. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs three times, all within two verses in Revelation 3:15–16. Those references establish where it appears, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force of the word there.

word:greek-nt:G2297.explanation: This word describes something marvelous or wonderful—something that awakens wonder and admiration. It expresses a strong positive response to what is seen or experienced, rather than merely saying that something is ordinary or pleasing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 21:15. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: the subject is remarkable and worthy of wonder.

word:greek-nt:G2309.explanation: Thelo means to desire or to will. It can also describe being willing to do something, as when someone is not willing to make another person a public example.

word:greek-nt:G2345.explanation: Thinganō means to touch or handle.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical fallback supports “temple,” but Mark 16:20 does not contain or directly support ἱερῷ or the stated sense. The entity identifier also conflates G2413 and G2411, so lexical identity is not preserved.

word:greek-nt:G2415.explanation: This word means “inhabitant of Jerusalem” or “of Jerusalem.” It identifies a person connected with that city, functioning as a designation for Jerusalem’s residents rather than naming a general spiritual quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 1:5 and John 7:25. Its precise reference in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a person from Jerusalem or associated with the city.

word:greek-nt:G2459.explanation: Ἰοῦστος is the name Justus, used as a surname.

word:greek-nt:G2576.explanation: Kammyō means to close or shut the eyes.

word:greek-nt:G2598.explanation: This verb describes bringing something down—either laying or throwing it down, or being struck down. Its central idea is downward movement or defeat, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament it occurs twice: once in 2 Corinthians and once in Hebrews. The two uses show that the word can describe a person being knocked down as well as the act of laying something down. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

word:greek-nt:G2657.explanation: Katanoeō means to perceive or discern something, and to consider it carefully.

word:greek-nt:G2785.explanation: Ketos means a huge sea fish, such as a whale.

word:greek-nt:G2820.explanation: This word expresses the idea of being “to be chosen” or “to obtain.” It points either to receiving something as one’s allotted portion or to being selected. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Ephesians 1:11. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns receiving an assigned portion or being chosen for one. It is not a broad term with many different uses in the New Testament.

word:greek-nt:G2914.explanation: Krete is the name of Crete.

word:greek-nt:G2958.explanation: This word is the personal name “Quirinius,” referring to a man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It functions as a proper name in the Greek New Testament and occurs once, in Luke 2:2. Because it identifies a person, its meaning is simply the individual’s name; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role in the event being described.

word:greek-nt:G2961.explanation: Kyrieuō means to have authority or rule over.

word:greek-nt:G3056.explanation: Logos means a word or speech. It can also refer to a divine utterance, as in the word of God.

word:greek-nt:G3081.explanation: This word means “to be advantageous” or “to profit.” It describes something as beneficial, worthwhile, or serving a person’s good rather than causing loss. The word is used once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 17:2, so its broader range cannot be traced through repeated passages. Its central idea remains the value or benefit gained from a situation, choice, or action. The surrounding verse is needed to show precisely how that idea functions there.

word:greek-nt:G3139.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “marble,” referring to the hard, polished stone used as a valuable building or decorative material. It functions as a noun naming a physical substance, not a person, action, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 18:12. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: marble, a costly stone associated with crafted or luxurious objects.

word:greek-nt:G3175.explanation: Megistan means a great man or a high-ranking noble.

word:greek-nt:G3434.explanation: Moloch is the name of a god worshipped by people.

word:greek-nt:G3478.explanation: Nazareth is the name of a city in Galilee. Jesus lived there.

word:greek-nt:G3513.explanation: This word means “as surely as” and functions as a firm affirmation or oath-like expression. It strengthens what the speaker is saying, emphasizing that the statement is certain and dependable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in 1 Corinthians 15:31. The word itself supplies emphasis rather than describing a person, object, or action. Its exact force in that verse is understood more fully from the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:greek-nt:G3706.explanation: Horasis means a sight or vision. It can also refer to an appearance—something seen.

word:greek-nt:G3863.explanation: Parazēloō means to provoke to jealousy.

word:greek-nt:G3889.explanation: Paramythia means comfort or consolation. It can also mean exhortation.

word:greek-nt:G3917.explanation: This word means “leopard,” referring to the swift, spotted wild animal. It is a noun naming an animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 13:2. The word’s basic meaning remains the animal itself; the significance of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its imagery, which are handled separately from the word’s ordinary lexical meaning.

word:greek-nt:G3980.explanation: Peitharcheō means to obey one in authority, following that person's direction.

word:greek-nt:G4013.explanation: Periagō means to go around. It can also mean to lead someone along.

word:greek-nt:G4141.explanation: Plēssō means to strike or smite.

word:greek-nt:G4178.explanation: Pollakis means many times, often, or frequently.

word:greek-nt:G4196.explanation: Poplios is the personal name Publius.

word:greek-nt:G4206.explanation: Porrō means far away or at a distance.

word:greek-nt:G4475.explanation: Rhapisma means a slap or blow on the cheek with the open hand.

word:greek-nt:G4556.explanation: Sardion means carnelian, a precious stone.

word:greek-nt:G4581.explanation: Seleucia is a proper name identifying a specific place. It is not a general quality, action, or description, but a place-name used to identify one location in the New Testament narrative. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Acts 13:4. The word itself supplies the name; the surrounding verse and passage provide the details about the place and its role in that account.

word:greek-nt:G4602.explanation: This word means “silence,” referring to the absence or stopping of speech and sound. It is a noun used in the Greek New Testament to describe quietness rather than spoken words. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Acts and once in Revelation. Its basic meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding passage determines whether the silence is public, temporary, or associated with a solemn moment.

word:greek-nt:G4750.explanation: Stoma means mouth, the physical opening through which food enters. It can also refer to speech, as when others hear a message through someone’s mouth. In another sense, it means the point or edge of a sword.

word:greek-nt:G4970.explanation: Sphodra means exceedingly, greatly, or very much.

word:greek-nt:G5069.explanation: Tetradion means a group of four soldiers.

word:greek-nt:G5083.explanation: Tēreō means to keep or observe commandments or a word, and it can also mean to guard or watch over someone.

word:greek-nt:G5292.explanation: Hypotagē means subjection, submission, or obedience.

word:greek-nt:G5410.explanation: Phoron means a forum or market.

word:greek-nt:G5487.explanation: Charitoō means to favor or to bestow freely on.
